newsitem.title: ITALY: Albania assures Italy it won't storm rebel towns.
newsitem.headline: Albania assures Italy it won't storm rebel towns.

text.p: Albania's President Sali Berisha has assured Italy that he will not use military force to retake southern towns held by armed rebels, Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said on Thursday.

Dini told reporters that Berisha had advised Italy that security forces acting under a state of emergency intended to isolate the towns and then try to negotiate with the rebels "to lay down their arms and return to a situation of normality".
"We have the government's assurances, and I hope they will be maintained, that the southern towns that are in the hands of rebels will not be taken by force," Dini said.
"We are being assured that they will not go beyond the surrounding, the isolating of the areas that are now out of the control of the government," he added.

Dini spoke after talks with Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, who will visit Albania on Friday for urgent talks with Berisha and the opposition on a European Union push for a political solution to the crisis.

Berisha, re-elected to second five-year term in office on Monday, is facing the worst crisis of his rule after insurgents in several southern towns looted police and army weapons depots over the weekend.

Undeterred by a state of emergency and shoot-on-sight orders for security forces, the insurgents hold sway in the southern port of Vlore, the Adriatic coastal town of Sarande and several other points where troops have faced stiff resistance.

A Reuter reporter said on Thursday that anti-government groups were also in firm control of the southern town of Tepelene where army officers had gone over to the rebel side and were calling for Berisha to resign.
Italy and Greece, points of refuge for Albanians in any mass exodus, have both expressed alarm about the unrest rocking the former Stalinist Balkan state, Europe's poorest country.

The Italian government said Prime Minister Romano Prodi again telephoned Berisha on Thursday urging him to restore conditions "for peaceful and democratic cooperation among all political forces" on how to tackle the crisis.
Prodi had also called on Berisha "to exercise great moderation and a sense of responsibility in matters of public order," the statement said.

Van Mierlo, whose country holds the EU's rotating presidency, was also visiting Athens later on Thursday for talks with the Greek government before travelling to Tirana on Friday to meet Berisha and opposition leaders.

The EU is pushing all sides in Albania to agree to form a government of national reconciliation and to refrain from exploiting the violence, unleashed by popular anger at the loss of savings in shady pyramid investment schemes.
The EU is Albania's biggest source of economic aid. Van Mierlo made clear that future support would be dependent on Albanian willingness to reach a political solution.
"We want to help (Albania) but they must make it possible," Van Mierlo said. He said a prerequisite for economic backing was that the EU and Albania agreed on the way to resolve the crisis.
